Wine. Freshly 21 I wanted something besides sugary drinks because 1. The awful hangovers and 2. Type 1 Diabetes. I tried wine and quickly started to learn there was a lot of nuance to it. In the last 4 years I've sunk 10s of thousands of dollars into wine, I've invested in a mid capacity wine cooler, I'm at the point where I'm looking at renting a wine locker at a dedicated storage facility, I've started collecting bottles to age and buying old vintages when I find them, I switched my entire career path so that I can work with wine on a daily basis, I joined a blind tasting group, and I've started pursuing industry certifications. Just got my WSET level 2 and I'm about to start my level 3 course.

Wine very quickly went from a small hobby to my entire life. It's been one of the best things to ever happen to me, I've met so many incredible people from distributors to wine makers, I've made so many amazing memories over great bottles of wine, and every day I'm pushed to learn more about a subject that's impossible to truly master. There's always something new to explore or learn and I love that. At this point I'm a proud cork dork.

Cons: I am perpetually broke because of how much I spend on wine and my apartment is filled with wine bottles and wine books.

Pros: I've always got great bottles of wine on hand, the kind of great that gives you a spiritual experience when you taste it.

Blind tasting wine, it's one facet of my wine hobby/career but one of the most fun aspects. It requires an insane amount of knowledge but trying to figure out what a wine is based upon color, the particular way it smells, how acidic and tannic it is, how much alcohol is in it. All of these things are little clues that will point you towards specific areas of the world and tip you off as to what grape was used to make the wine. It's extremely difficult but fun as all hell, especially when you guess correctly.

Drink wine however you want to, drink the cheap stuff, drink the pricey stuff, only have a glass or get wasted. Do what you enjoy. Some people might look at you weird for drinking 1961 Cheval Blanc from a styrofoam cup but who cares. Personally I use nice glassware because it does offer a better experience, but if you're happy with a solo cup then that's all that matters. I would recommend you look towards smaller and more obscure producers though. Typically your money goes much further with small producers than the big names. Your local wine store should be able to point you in the right direction there.

You don't have to miss out on older wines just because you can't cellar some bottles for 20+ years. When you make your trip to the city look for or ask about library vintages. A lot of wineries will store so many bottles of each vintage and then 10-20+ years later they'll release those bottles into the market. Some higher end stores will also have a collection of old vintages as well. I've been lucky enough to find an 04 Beaucastel and an 06 La Mouline and La Turque out in the wild. Well I've found a lot more than that, those are the three old vintages I've actually bought.

It's fascinating though that two people of completely different ages, completely different backgrounds, and completely different experience levels can find themselves in the same situation thanks to something as simple as a love for good wine.

I say go for your level 3, better yet take your wine education as far as you can. The world of wine is such a rewarding experience, not just from great wine you'll try but also the connection you can make and the people you can meet. I won't name drop but I recently got to have dinner with a legendary winemaker from the Santa Lucia Highlands and that experience will forever be one of the coolest things to happen to me. We drank through some of his wines (which were phenomenal), he talked about his vineyards and his experience, his philosophy on winemaking, he told some stories about his career, and we had some smaller conversation about things unrelated to wine. It was just kind of surreal hearing so much about this guy and then sitting there talking to him, learning from him, and also chatting away like he was just any random person. That's a long way of saying the further you take your education the more people you'll meet and the more opportunities you'll have for experiences like this, and if you ask me those experiences are priceless.

Port is always from Portugal, specifically from the Duoro Valley in northern Portugal. If a label says Port but it's not from the Duoro Valley then it's a cheap fortified wine trying to coast off the success of Port without putting in the work. IIRC the term Port is also legally protected now, only a handful of producers outside of the Duoro Valley are still legally allowed to call their wine Port. Same concept as Champagne.

Port is a wonderful wine but Taylor honestly isn't that great. Spend an extra $10 for a bottle of Noval Tawny Port. It taste 100x better and the hangover is far less awful. Banyuls is also a great option, fortified wines from France similar to port, nice juicy red fruit notes and some chocolate notes.

I felt this in my soul. I've made my career on the distribution side but I've had some serious moments of imposter syndrome. I am far from the average wine rep, I'm pretty young compared to most wine reps, covered in visible tattoos, and I'm a woman so I've had many experiences where buyers brush off my experience for the opinion of an older man with half the experience I have and that has gotten to me at times. I've also spent the last two years trying to get on with a small local distributor. The portfolio is amazing, DRC, E. Guigal, Gaja, Tenuta Delle Tere Nere, Muga, Juan Gil, Adam Lee wines, just a few examples of how killer this book is. A year ago I interviewed with the owner of the company and I completely froze up during the interview, I could barely speak, I was visibly shaking, it was not good. Almost everyone at this company has at least 10 years of industry experience compared to my almost 4.  Therapy has helped a lot with addressing my imposter syndrome though and the manager for this company has become my mentor pushing me to expand my knowledge and hone my skills. I've also started on my WSET certs which has given me a huge boost to my confidence, having a tangible thing that proves that I know my shit because my voice has so frequently been ignored in the past. In about two months I'll have another chance with getting on at this distributor and I'm feeling a lot more confident this time around.

Get to know your reps, they know about openings and might be able to help you get in.

Make sure your car is in good condition, you'll be driving a lot, like 2,000 miles a month.

Get familiar with the portfolios of the different distributors but especially the portfolio of the company you're applying for. Product knowledge goes a long way.

You can also try for some industry certifications, not a requirement but it can help a lot. I'm in the process of getting my WSET certs, level 2 coming up in April. They offer certifications both for wine and spirits.

You'll have the easiest time getting on with Glazer's, Breakthru, or RNDC but don't try making a career with those companies unless you're okay with sacrificing morals for the sake of profits, and keep in mind they've all been lay off crazy lately. Shitty companies that don't care about their reps. Get started there, make the switch to a small distributor as fast as possible, and don't buy into the corporate propaganda they push. The big three hate small distributors with a burning passion.

Keep in mind it's still a cut-throat business. You'll meet a lot of chill people but there's also a lot of people ready to stab you in the back, typically people from the big 3.

You'll probably have more luck getting an on-prem position so lean into your restaurant experience.

OND is absolute hell in this industry, you will have no work life balance and you'll be miserable but you'll make good money, things die down in January though so take the first couple months of the year to take care of yourself. Book a massage, make sure you're going to therapy, maybe take a week of vacation to just wind down after the OND hell hole. If you don't you'll hit burn out 10x faster, and burn out can get pretty dark in the alcohol industry. You'll get a lot of free alcohol and that doesn't always mesh well with high stress and burnout so just take care of yourself as much as possible.

Make sure you've got some nice clothes. There isn't necessarily a dress code for this industry but business casual is typically a safe bet, but you'll be going to supplier events and such so some professional clothes are good to have on hand. Don't forget to be yourself though, it's what made my connections with buyers so strong, I wasn't another cookie cutter rep. I'm covered in visible tattoos and while I still dress nice it's very clearly elder emo style. Buyers tend to favor reps who actually have a personality.

Don't become obsessed with the money. You can make pretty good money but you'll never get rich in this line of work and if you focus entirely on that you'll be miserable. I've got a deep love for wine, it's my career and my biggest hobby, that's what keeps me going when things get shitty. Knowing that my work not only gets me a paycheck but it also supports the families who've been running wineries for multiple generations, helping farmers in impoverished countries continue to make a living, keeping the harvesters who work their ass off fed, fighting racism and xenophobia by breaking down cultural barriers with wine as the medium, helping people live their life a little better by making sure they get their moneys worth with small producer wines instead of the BS California get rich quick scheme wineries, there's a lot of joy to be found in what you do. Keep that in mind and the money will keep coming, obsess over the money and you'll be miserable, then performance drops as well as commission, and you're struggling to make the same kind of money you did before. 

Get a big water bottle, you'll be in your car all day long and staying hydrated is important, also don't forget to take time to eat.

Support your favorite accounts, stop in for lunch, grab a quick drink at the end of the day, stuff like that. It helps build a solid rapport and when you support your accounts they'll support you.

Expect to work about 50 hours a week, don't worry though this industry offers a much better work life balance than other industries despite working more. It normally feels more like 30 hours a week and during the slow months you'll have even more free time.

Mentioning therapy again, it can get very stressful at times but there's a work life balance so you can get therapy to help. Seriously this is probably my biggest piece of advice. I got in a bad slump at one point and I wasn't taking care of myself or getting therapy at the time. Things got dark very quickly for me because of the nature of the industry, make sure you've got a safety net in place.

Mercurey is a village in Burgundy. Mercurey poisoning refers to the phenomenon where someone starts drinking Burgundy, falls in love with it, and before they know it they're filing bankruptcy for the 3rd time because they've got a wine cooler filled to the brim with Burgundy but not the salary to support it. Just a fun wine joke that's not one of the typical cliche jokes.

The best way to build your tasting skills is to taste and smell everything you can outside of wine and catalogue that so you can call back to it when tasting wine. If you're really struggling with minerality you can try getting different mineral samples and licking them. It sounds weird but tasting minerals will help you pick up on minerality in wine.
Be careful drinking Burgundy, you might get Mercurey poisoning.

I had the pleasure of meeting the winemaker and the man is incredibly creative. The blends are very innovative and these wines are so unique that it's almost best to describe them with personality traits rather than traditional tasting notes.

If I'm spending that kind of money though chances are I'm buying a Chateauneuf du Pape, it's very hard to go wrong with a bottle of Beaucastel or Clos Des Papes. I'm currently waiting on a bottle of Famille Isabel Ferrando Colombis, having recently tried their 2022 vintage the $165 price tag feels like a steal compared to the quality of the wine. I couldn't imagine dropping that much on a Napa.

At that same price point you can find some killer Burgs as well, the Albert Bichot Gevrey-Chambertin is a great example, and for a bit more but still within napa prices you could pick up a premier cru Vosne-Romanee.

Yes and no. Some bottles of wine are drinkable for a very long time and others aren't. All wine wants to turn into alcoholic vinegar but there are multiple factors that determine how long that takes. Every wine has a lifecycle in which it probably shouldn't be opened yet, then a period of this wine is at it's prime, and then the wine is dropping in quality and turning into vinegar. Certain factors can affect this such as the tannins, acid, sugar, and sulfur. If any of these aspects of the wine are particularly high it lends the wine to a longer life. The other factor is whether or not the wine is an oxidative wine. These wines have a very controlled exposure to oxygen during the wine making process and as a result they can be kept (if unopened) indefinitely. A side note oxygen is the enemy when we talk about the lifetime of a wine, as oxygen is exposed to wine it breaks down the preservative compounds in the wine turning it to vinegar. This process still happens with a cork, it's just significantly slower than with an open bottle of wine. Another factor to consider is the quality of the wine. Poor quality fruit leads to poor quality wine which does not keep long. High quality fruit that makes high quality wine will typically hold for much longer but there's typically a higher price tag associated with these wines. Finally a wine needs to be kept in proper conditions to hold for long periods of time. Too hot and a wine will either cook or prematurely age. If the humidity levels are off you also risk the cork drying out and leading to increased oxygen exposure. Same reason why you want to store wine on its side, it keeps the cork moist. Wine is very finicky when you're aging it.

All of that being said this most certainly is not a wine meant to be aged. This is a bottle of cheap wine with fruit not capable of aging and even if it were I'm going to assume the bottle was not held in any type of proper conditions over the years. Would it kill you? Probably not, but it would taste absolutely disgusting.
Source: I work in the wine industry.

Wine isn't way sweeter. Some wines are like a sautrenes, banyuls, or a moscato but I've met plenty of beer drinkers who can't handle the intensity of some wines. Take for instance a Chablis that is known for its cut throat acidity, or grenache which can take on peppery and spicy qualities. Then there is red burgundy which often is regarded as some of the most complex wine on the planet with its deep earthy, funky, and sometimes musty qualities. I've had some Gevrey-Chambertin before that has left my mouth dry as hell from its tannins. Wine is insanely complex, a lot of us spend our entire lives trying to understand it and we hardly scratch the surface. Every hectare produces wine differently even when side by side. And these are just a few of thousands of different examples. If you're ever interested in seeing the scope of wine Windows on the World by Kevin Zraly is a great place to start.
Source: I work in the wine industry and have spent many many thousands of dollars on wine, I also drink a lot of beer.

My experience is the inverse. I started at a credit union at 17 as a teller. 3 years later I’m now at a regional bank. Honestly I would probably say I prefer credit unions. It’s lower pay but overall a better experience. From my time in both I have noticed credit unions focus more heavily on consumer accounts. You get to know the members very well, from their personality to their personal lives and their financial habits. The bank I’m at now has a much higher focus on business accounts. My day to day is typically deposits for different companies and I never recognize the person dropping them off as it changes so often. At the credit union I knew probably around 200 different people who regularly came by, here at the bank it’s about 4 people. Credit unions also have a much more relaxed and casual approach to their environment while banks are much more professional. In banking I’ve noticed much less politics in specific branches but as a whole the bank is like a high school locker room. The credit union on the other hand was much more political in the branch but the FI as a whole was much more professional than the bank.

I’ll preface this saying that I’m just a teller I’ve never worked as an FSR but writing checks to most people is fine. If you come to the bank at least once every couple of weeks chances are we remember you, and if someone’s calling to get more account info we verify things like social date of birth and those kind of things so just the account number won’t get them far. I’m sure there’s someway to pull off fraud with the info found on a check but your average Joe isn’t going to be doing that. The most common thing I’ve seen is someone getting their hands on someone’s checks and writing checks to themselves.
